```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.2, fig.height = 4.2, dpi = 96,
                      out.width = "100%", message = FALSE)
```

A field border is often hard to see in one satellite image: two fields of the same crop
can look alike on any given day. Over a season the border becomes obvious, because
neighbouring fields are sown, irrigated, cut and harvested at different times. The
**temporal boundary contrast** (TBC) method in `fieldborders` uses this. For pairs of
pixels on either side of a known border and pairs inside one field, it measures how
differently every band and normalised difference changes between the two pixels over a
year of monthly Sentinel-2 images, ranks the features by how well this contrast separates
the two kinds of pairs, and learns from the best of them:

* an **edge map**, the probability that a pixel lies on a border between two fields, and
* a **cropland map**, the probability that a pixel belongs to a field at all.

Field objects are then grown from seeds inside fields by a marker-controlled watershed on
the edge map. The maps can be fused with the output of a deep segmentation model, and the
result is scored with the object metric of the Fields of The World (FTW) benchmark.

```{r}
library(fieldborders)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
```

## A Sentinel-2 time series

The package ships four small windows (about 1 km across) of monthly Sentinel-2 scenes,
ten bands each, on the FTW grid of about 5 m. This one is in the Columbia Basin of
Washington, with centre-pivot and rectangular irrigated fields:

```{r}
s <- fb_example_stack("washington")
s
```

```{r, fig.height = 2.6}
months <- c(3, 5, 7, 9)
wrap_plots(lapply(months, function(k) fb_plot_rgb(s, date = k) + labs(subtitle = NULL)), nrow = 1)
```

Your own images enter the same way through `fb_read_stack()` (one multi-band file per
date) or `fb_stack()` (a `SpatRaster`), and `fb_s2_monthly()` downloads a monthly series for
any area (see `vignette("new-area")`).

## Edge and cropland maps

`fb_model_pretrained()` returns models fitted on reference fields in California and
Washington. `fb_tbc_maps()` applies a model to a stack:

```{r}
m <- fb_model_pretrained("general")
m
maps <- fb_tbc_maps(s, m)
```

```{r, fig.height = 4}
fb_plot_maps(maps)
```

## From maps to fields

`fb_delineate()` turns the maps into field objects, with the thresholds that were tuned
for the model on separate reference tiles:

```{r}
m$thresholds
fields <- fb_delineate(maps, thresholds = m$thresholds)
```

```{r, fig.height = 5}
fb_plot_fields(fields, s, date = 7)
```

`fb_polygons()` converts the objects to an `sf` data frame with the area, perimeter,
compactness and mean map values of each field, ready to be written to any vector format:

```{r}
p <- fb_polygons(fields, maps)
head(p)
f <- tempfile(fileext = ".gpkg")
sf::st_write(p, f, quiet = TRUE)
```

`fb_fields()` runs the same steps in one call.

## How good is it?

The California example comes with reference fields from the California Department of
Water Resources. `fb_reference()` rasterises them to the image grid (field interior,
boundary, background), and `fb_evaluate()` matches delineated and reference fields one to
one at an intersection over union above 0.5, as in the FTW benchmark:

```{r}
s_ca <- fb_example_stack("california")
f_ca <- fb_example_files("california")
ref_poly <- sf::st_read(f_ca$fields, quiet = TRUE)
ref <- fb_reference(ref_poly, s_ca)
maps_ca <- fb_tbc_maps(s_ca, m)
fields_ca <- fb_delineate(maps_ca, thresholds = m$thresholds)
ev <- fb_evaluate(ref, fields_ca)
fb_accuracy(ev)[, c("reference_fields", "predicted_fields", "obj_precision", "obj_recall", "obj_f1")]
```

```{r, fig.height = 5}
fb_plot_fields(fields_ca, s_ca, date = 7, reference = ref_poly)
```

The dashed white lines are the reference fields. A window this small holds only a few
fields, so these numbers say little about accuracy in general; `vignette("validation")`
summarises the validation on several thousand reference fields.

## Adding a deep model

Deep segmentation models such as the FTW PRUE models predict, for every pixel, the
probability of background, field interior and field boundary from two images of the
season. `fb_prue_predict()` runs PRUE in R (it needs the `torch` package); the examples
include its output for each window:

```{r}
dl <- fb_read_probabilities(f_ca$prue)
fu <- fb_model_pretrained("general", "fusion")
fused <- fb_fuse(maps_ca, dl, fu)
```

The fusion combines the deep-model and TBC probabilities with two logistic regressions
fitted on reference pixels. The three edge maps side by side:

```{r, fig.height = 3}
edges <- c(dl[["boundary"]], maps_ca[["edge"]], fused[["edge"]])
names(edges) <- c("PRUE B3", "TBC", "TBC + PRUE B3")
fb_plot_maps(edges)
```

and the accuracy of the objects obtained from each, all with the same object procedure
(the deep model alone with the thresholds of the fusion):

```{r, fig.height = 3}
counts <- rbind(
  cbind(method = "PRUE B3", fb_evaluate(ref, fb_delineate(dl, thresholds = fu$thresholds))),
  cbind(method = "TBC", fb_evaluate(ref, fields_ca)),
  cbind(method = "TBC + PRUE B3", fb_evaluate(ref, fb_delineate(fused, thresholds = fu$thresholds))))
fb_plot_accuracy(fb_accuracy(counts, by = "method"))
```
